mappings.name: a merchant's receiver that acknowledges six seconds late

why: THE ONLY WAY a test can be sure a worker is mid-delivery when it signals it.
worker_kill9.rs's third scenario sends SIGTERM to a worker whose deliver_webhook
job is inside its POST, and 'inside' has to be an interval something outside the
process can observe: WireMock journals a request when it MATCHES it, before it
serves any fixedDelayMilliseconds, so POST /__admin/requests/count reports this
request while the sender is still blocked on the response. Same technique, and
the same justification, as the mtn tree's requesttopay-kill9.json.
SIX SECONDS, and the number is chosen against two shipping budgets rather than
against a stopwatch. It is BELOW vpay_worker::webhooks::WEBHOOK_REQUEST_TIMEOUT
(10 s), so the acknowledgement always arrives before the delivery client's own
deadline and the drain has something to finish; and it is BELOW the worker's
--shutdown-grace-seconds in that test (20 s), so the drain can never run out of
time. Both comparisons are const assertions in worker_kill9.rs against the
shipping constants, so lowering either budget breaks the build rather than
making that test flaky.
A DEDICATED PATH, not a delay on /webhooks: tests/webhooks.rs asserts exact
ladder timings against this same receiver tree, and a six-second pause on the
path it uses would slow every one of those tests and improve none of them.
Priority 1 beats any-post-200.json's catch-all (priority 10) on this path only,
which is also why nothing else in the repository -- including compose.e2e.yml's
wiremock-webhook, which mounts this same directory -- sees any change.
200 with a JSON body for the same reason the catch-all has one: handle_deliver
treats any 2xx as delivered and records the first part of the body in
webhook_deliveries.response_excerpt, which an operator reads.
